Age of Mythology is the classic, mythology based spinoff of Age of Empires, and boy was it fun. But does Age of Mythology  Extended Edition live up to the original? In many ways, very much so, though the price tag might dissaude you unless you're a huge fan, (like I am). 

If you've played Age of Mythology before, you know exactly how this game works. If not, here a basic gist of it. It plays much like Age of Empires 2; you have to collect resources, specifically food, wood and gold, in order to fund your armies, economies, technologies and advancement. sounds basic enough, and all the races work similarly in regards to these resources. The difference comes in the fourth resource: Favour. Favour is generated differently depending on which race you are playing. For instance, the greeks generate favour through worship, the egyptians through building monuments, the norse through heroes and fighting, and the atlanteans through having more settlements. 

Favour is the special resource, which ties into the major mechanic of Age of Mythology: Gods and God Powers. There are 12 major gods, 3 for each of the races, and these determine starting bonuses for you when you start the game. the gods also have minor gods to choose each time you advance an age, with a total of 36 minor gods, each offering different bonuses and god powers. For instance Hades gives you the Sentinel God Power, that creates stone sentinels to watch over your town centre, but in the second age, you can choose Athena, who allows you to train minotaurs and the Restoration God power which can heal your units.

Aside from the new favour mechanic, for the major part it plays like the age of empires games. Build Army, upgrade, and take care of your population cap and economy. Rock paper scissors, for basic units, (cavalry beats archers who beat infantry), but add heroes and myth units which can turn the tide of battle. Both the singleplayer and multiplayer are fun, and with the new release, there is a rebirth in the multiplayer, though not as big as the heyday of AoM. 

As being essentially a remake (a la Age of Empires 2 HD Edition), AoM:EE is actually fairly bug free, and while it definitely shows its age, the added subtle lighting effects, water and shadows do help to make look better. It is definitely very playable, and for fans of the original, it shouldn't even be a bother.

The campaign is just as memeroable as always, a hunt through Greece, Egypt, Scandinavia and finally Atlantis in order to stop a power hungry cyclops from releasing Kronos, King of the Titans; followed by A New Atlantis, set a number of years later, [spoiler] where you are tricked into releasing the Titans, and must stop them at all costs [/spoiler]. 

Overall, Age of Mythology: Extended Editon is fun, unique and offers up plenty of value, with 50 singleplayer missions, skrimishes, and now revived multiplayer, though for those who still have a copy of Age of Mythology and The Titans expansion, it might not add a great deal. Definitely recommend everyone else (who's a fan of older RTSes).

First of all, I love Age of Mythology.  I played it way more than any other "Age Of" game as a kid and the game itself, along with the original 2003 "The Titans" expansion, is an underappreciated gem.  This Steam Extended Edition and the new Tale of the Dragon expansion is unbalanced and flawed.

There are a number of changes that really affect the gameplay, such as the new day/night cycle which Egypt makes use of.  Unfortunately, the day/night cycle looks really bad and makes it very hard to actually see what's going on at times as the day/night cycle plunges you into darkness.  The new units that have been added for each Civ feel very unbalanced and completely out of character with the original Civs.  I don't know who thought every civ needed a healer unit or that the Atlanteans needed an onager but it really doesn't work. 

The enemy AI ranges from absolutely braindead to IBM Deep Blue in skill, often in a single game.  I played with an AI ally on medium and it never moved its army once, it never built other town centres or even used the Titan it had made.  It sat completely still, and the enemy AI did the same thing.  On maps like New World or ones where you start on islands, an AI on Easy won't even build boats, transport units, it won't even fight back.  In contrast, the AI on hard and Titan just seems to know the location of everything on the map and works with Skynet like precision.  The AI makes really odd decisions, attacks in bizarre ways and won't utilise the maps or miracles to its advantage. 

On that similar note, pathfinding can be really awful at times, with your units taking the longest way possible to get to targets.  They get hung up on trees and rocks, get stuck on each other.  Sometimes units will ignore something shooting at them to focus fire on a villager or a random house.  Walking your titan into a crowded base is agony, it circles entire buildings to attack the same building from a designated "spot".

The new civilization, China, feels very odd to play.  Their miracles are really boring to use, with little imagination put into their design,, and their civilisation play-style has you clicking between buildings half the time.  Their upgrades are spread out across multiple buildings and they seem both weak and overpowered depending on the situation and map.  I can't tell what situation or map they excel in as they're pretty poorly designed and the units have bad visual design to distinguish them from other units, are poorly voice and seem to be reskins of other units from better civs.  It's a shame, given there's a great idea at the core of this civ.  You also can't turn this China civ off at all, and you are basically forced to play with the Tale of the Dragon DLC to get the full Age of Mythology experience.  That's right, Tale of the Dragon is COMPULSORY.

The population cap is much lower than the other Age of Empires game and this really hurts AoM.  You can't build up a nice large army and duke it out, and you'll hit the pop cap very quickly as the vanilla civs (Greeks, Egyptians, Norse) and almost instantly as the Atlanteans. It limits your ability to experiment and play around in combat.  I have a feeling this may be a product of the awful Netcode, as the game chugs when two armies clash.  Get three together and it looks like the game runs in Powerpoint.  On that note, the online servers and matchmaking abilities are limited and the Netcode is pretty rubbish.  There is constant stuttering as units move across the move, they jerk around, and this makes control in the heat of battle awful.  Expect lag and desyncs at the worst of times, and memory issues on longer games.

Don't get me wrong, you can have a fun time here.  My friends and I have a blast playing this due to how unbalanced it is, with some God Powers being just so fun to use, and others making us scratch our heads laughing.  If you can look past the many flaws introduced by the Extended Edition, you'll have a fun time.  But at $42.95 AUD?  Just get it on sale, that's way way way too much to pay.

This is a flawed version of a brilliant game.  This game really could benefit from the treatment that AoE 1 and AoE 2 got with their Definitive Editions.  A careful restoration with appropriate balancing, AI, pathfinding, and even some future civilisations like maybe the Aztec, India, Japan, could really inject new life into this game.  As it stands, this is a buggy release of a classic.

Ordinarily, I don't write reviews - but I've always been pretty invested in the Ensemble Studios games and seeing what Microsoft and Skybox have done with one of their all-time legends has pushed me into comment.

Age of Mythology: Extended Edition. Ordinarily, to extend something means to prolong it or make it bigger somehow but if you're hoping for new content, this game does not have any. It's just the same game you played back in 2003 - but that's not so bad, because that game was great. This however, isn't - and there's some vital reasons as to why:

1 - The Multiplayer.
 The most important aspect of any Real Time Strategy game is its multiplayer community and Age of Mythology has always had a creative and thriving one. This Extended Edition would too - if the multiplayer actually worked. You don't need me to tell you, just go check out the Support forum for this game. The game suffers from consistent crashes, desync, stuttering, framedrops and lag when attempting an online game. The developers blame "ancient bugs" left over from the original game despite the fact that none of these bugs were actually present in the 2003 release and accusing the now defunct Ensemble Studios (thanks Microsoft) for being responsible for your own mistakes is downright cowardly. disrespectful and lazy especially seeing as you're now flogging their product to an unaware market.

2 - The Single Player.
 The AI during Single Player matches is bizarre, eclectic and at often times completely incomprehensible. Prone to suddenly stopping all activity halfway through a match for completely banal reasons (there was no food in their line of sight, you spawned too close to them etc) every Random Match is essentially a roll-of-the-dice of whether or not the AI feels like playing along this time. This problem has only been made worse by the addition of the new, COMPULSORY DLC which has 'updated' the AI to coincide with the introduction of a new civilization. Unfortunately, those who don't purchase the DLC are still obligated to download the patch, meaning they suffer from all of the bugs whilst receiving none of the reward.

3 - The DLC.
  Most likely what drew you to this Steam page in the first place seeing as this game hasn't seen a real increase in playerbase in almost a year. I followed the development of the DLC for a good few months and have been heavily invested in it. The attitude of the developers and their 'effort' as far as producing quality content goes is detestable. Aside from the rather invested and community-involved attitude from those at ForgottenEmpires (a small team of fans), comment and involvement from the lead developers (Skybox) has consisted of grade-1 piss-all. They spent a good few months assuring us the DLC would contain strictly new, fresh content without any reskinning, repackaging or rebranding of existing content and that turned out to be a complete lie. They also lied about having playtested the game for balance - admitting during a public streaming of the game (you can find it on Youtube) that they purposefully left the DLC broken and unbalanced as a means of making people have to play it. The DLC itsels is incredibly broken as of writing this (again, check the Support forum), with half the playerbase unable to access the DLC at all and the other half jokingly trying to laugh off the regret of their purchase.

One of the developers admitted on the Subreddit that they are currently "using the public to beta test the game" - meaning that if you buy this DLC you are not getting content, you are buying into the opportunity to test unfinished content. This coupled with the fact that the developers openly laughed at the idea of fixing the Multiplayer (again, check the stream) tells me that we aren't dealing with incompetent developers - we're dealing with scam artists.

I don't like having to write this sort of stuff about any Ensemble Studios IP because it sucks seeing their legacy shat on by untalented coat-tail riders, but if it means discouraging people from wasting their money on what is essentially a gigantic bug test, then it feels somewhat worthwhile. Only buy this if you absolutely *must* play Age of Mythology again and don't want to go through the effort of pirating the old copy and getting it to work - but know that this is not the Age of Mythology you played ten years ago and it certainly is not a well-supported or active game.

Age of Mythology (AOM) is, in my opinion, the best game in the Age of Empires series. The idea to syncretize ancient civilizations with their gods intervening with their powers and mythological units was brilliant. The human soldiers being grabbed by a cyclops, legs desperatly moving in the air, and then being tossed back into his friends while knocking down trees gives a sentiment of helplessness against the superhuman forces of the mythic creatures in place in this universe. The gods also help the humans, providing healing or thicker armor; acting in favor of their economies by providing a prosperous harvest, rain or even attacking the enemy's economy with locust swarms that eat every farm on their sight (and even the villagers on their way). 

The gameplay is fairly dynamic, with battles being fought with large armies quite quickly instead of a long and protracted building phase as in older RTS games. This almost straight to action approach, with buildings being destroyed by the troops way faster than in earlier games in the series (with the also fast capacity for rebuilding them) gives Age of Mythology a more dramatic and fast-paced gameplay. Buildings aren't all powerful fortified obstacles that can only be breached by siege weapons (they do help, but are not essential) but they can form a fortified position when mutually supported by troops. The human soldiers fight in rock-paper-scissors counters: infantry with lances beat cavalry, who beats archers, that in turn beat infantry; plus specialized troops augmenting or changing such roles (archers beat infantry, but the fast running Huskarl will close-in fast and kill them). The mythological units are powerful but there are heroes in the game that will counter them. The same principle applies to naval warfare. 

On the economic field, you have food, wood, gold and favour. While the first three are self-explanatory, favour is especific to this game and plays a great role: it is the protection your civilization receive from the gods. Each faction has a different way of gaining favour: the Greeks pray at the temple while the Egyptians build monuments. Each civilization has three major gods that will affect it in a particular way. At each Age you have to choose a minor god to advance, granting you a special power and a different myth unit. Gods also provide different research improvements and almost all of them cost favor. The game revolves around building and mantaining city centers, that not only provide the training of villagers, but also increase your population count  and need to be built in especific and limited places; making it an strategic objective in-game.

The game has five campaigns but only the original one is good. The community does not allow discussions and is very weak in guides. Strategies, build orders... all of this must be researched outside Steam. Another problem is the lack of balance. The first expansion added the Atlanteans, that are awfully overpowered. They do not need to build resource depots (the mark of lazy design), they do not need to build any especific building for gaining favour (their city centers automatically generate favour), their buildings are stronger than everybody's and their villagers are small tanks with far more hitpoints - any of their units can become heroes... The Norse are the only ones to build heroes in unlimited numbers already on the Archaic Age and this leads to very cheap early rushes. The major god Loki summons myth units for Norse heroes fighting, so it is no surprise so many players pick this god. The Chinese, while not a bad faction, had such a lazy campaign, with boring missions and awfully crude cinematics (worse than the ones on the AOM original release)! Worse, the Chinese expansion changes the menu presentation and the theme music - which I hated - and does not provide an option for the traditional menu.

With those problems aside (like few people still playing the game), AOM is a great experience and I still to this day get a smile when I listen to the songs and sounds of this game (Prostagma?). The original campaign is a Tour de Force following the hero Arkantos and his friends through the myths of the ancient Greeks, Egyptians and Norse; with you fighting the Trojan War with Ajax and the like under the guidance of Athena. The visuals are great, with the gods of AOM being among the best portrayals of those mythical figures that I have ever seen. Playing this game with friends, even against the AI, is always garanteed fun. Highly recommended.

Glorious game from the good old days.

Back when I was little, Age of Mythology and its expansion, defined my childhood. I could never beat Age of Empires II because of its difficulty, but somehow, Age of Mythology offered me a fair chance. Its presentation, game mechanics and atmosphere were unique at the time.

Right from the start, the ancient Greek theme of the game attracted me and the mission design, the peaceful music and the gorgeous graphics, made a big impression on me.

In Age of Mythology, you play as three different cultures. The game revolves around the hero Arkantos, an Antaltean war hero that has been ordered to assist the Greek in their fight against the Trojans. Before his departure, the Trident of Poseidon gets stolen. He retrieves it and sets sail to Troy. He assists the Greek, rescues the Centaur Chiron, and the war is won, however his ship is damaged too much for the return trip home to Atlantis.

Arkantos learns of many prisoners that are being held in the underworld, which has been opened via an entrance, that was been built by prisoner slave labour, by the Cyclops Warlord Gargarensis. Arkantos and Chiron destroy his base of operations and pursue the Cyclops, which escapes via the Underworld. Arkantos eventually ends up in Egypt, via one of the Underworld Entrances.

Arkantos learns the motives of Gargarensis, which is achieving immortality through freeing Kronos. This must be stopped at all costs. He sides with the Egyptians and together they must find the scattered body parts of Osiris, which is powerful enough to stop the Cyclops from achieving his goal. The parts are found, Osiris is summoned and destroys Gargarensis’ entire army. The beast himself however, escaped yet again via the Underworld entrance.

They pursue him towards the Nordic lands and are greeted by the hostility of the Norse God Loki, who deceives and tricks the local chieftains to attack Arkantos and his men on sight. After the trickery is discovered, the Norsemen side with Arkantos in pursue of Gargarensis and track him down in the Nifilheim, the Norse underworld. A glorious battle takes place and Gargarensis is captured and beheaded.

Arkantos sails back to Atlantis, only to discover that Loki struck again and the head of Gargarensis is actually that of Kemsyt's, the general of Gargarensis. The Cyclops is still alive and is closing in on the prison that holds Kronos. Zeus, who has observed the mighty deeds of Arkantos, grants him God like powers and with his new skills, he initiated the final battle with Gargarensis and defeats him. He dies however because of inflicted injuries, but is revived by Athena, who makes him a God.

Just epic.

The campaign was a lot of fun and I enjoyed every mission. Of course, the various cheats were hilarious and back then, it was just unrealistic and mind-blowing to see a bear with a Canada cape shooting lasers out of its eyes, appear out of nowhere after stroking some keys in a textbox. The same goes off course for the car in Age of Empires II.

I really enjoyed the changes of scenery and units in the different cultures throughout the game. Details like the native language the units speak, the many cryptids and units of legends like Centaurs, Anubis and Minotaur’s, really enhanced the experience.

When talking graphics, this game looked/looks amazing. Units and buildings are very detailed and the landscapes and maps are so colorful and alive. The move and combat animations of the units are also spot on. Back then, I thought Age Of Mythology was one of the best looking games I played.

The sound and music is also a piece of art. The calm ambient music is very memorable and is perfectly fitted for the culture that you are playing in that mission. The sound effects and voice overs for the units are also spot on. It is sound design at its best.

Control wise, the game plays identical to Age of Empires II, but a little easier. I cannot explain why exactly, but I just thought the interfaces and tutorial were a little more “noob friendly”.

The expansion, Age of Mythology: The Titans, was also a work of art. In this expansion, you play as the Atlanteans, an advanced civilization that was far ahead of the Greek, Norse and Egyptian people.

In short, in the campaign revolves around the Titan Kronos, which is still imprisoned in Tartarus after many years. From his prison, he watches Atlantis fall and the survivors trying to stay alive in the Norse wilderness. Kronos sends out one of his demi-god servants and possesses a guy named Krios, forcing him to do his bidding and stirring the Atlantean civilization towards freeing him.

The Atlanteans arrive at a resourceful island and rebuild their civilization, while being deceived that Kronos granted them all of this. In turn, they are convinced to worship Kronos as their God. This angers the other civilizations of Egypt, Greece and the Nords. They go to war with Atlantis, a war that Atlantis wins decisively. The Atlanteans then destroy the Nordic kingdom, attack Egypt and wreak havoc upon the world.

Eventually, the Atlanteans discover the treachery of Krios and the deception of Kronos. They change sides and the Atlantean leader Kastos fights other Atlanteans under Kronos’ control and eventually, battles Kronos himself with the help of Titans and his Greek allies. Krios is killed and Kastos receives The Staff of Atlantis, and he and is people rebuild their civilization in peace.

The introduction of the new Atlantean race, units and story, was a great new experience and back then, it was just as refreshing and unique as the base game.

The expansion also added new features like training units infinitely, as long as you have the sufficient resources. It also granted the power to summon a Titan to bring death and destruction to your enemies.

I enjoyed every mission of Age of Mythology: The Titans and still think this is one of the best additions to a game in a long line of personal played DLC.

Overall, this is one of those games that takes me back to my childhood, a happy time without worries. Just me and Age of Mythology. It will always remain a classic and one of the better games I played back then.

Definitely recommend this gem.

[h1]Long version:[/h1]
Age of Mythology (AOM) is, in my opinion, the best game in the Age of Empires series. The idea to synchronize ancient civilizations with their gods intervening with their powers and mythological units was brilliant. The human soldiers being grabbed by a cyclops, legs desperately moving in the air, and then being tossed back into his friends while knocking down trees gives a sentiment of helplessness against the superhuman forces of the mythic creatures in place in this universe. The gods also help the humans, providing healing or thicker armor; acting in favor of their economies by providing a prosperous harvest, rain or even attacking the enemy's economy with locust swarms that eat every farm on their sight (and even the villagers on their way).

The game play is fairly dynamic, with battles being fought with large armies quite quickly instead of a long and protracted building phase as in older RTS games. This almost straight to action approach, with buildings being destroyed by the troops way faster than in earlier games in the series (with the also fast capacity for rebuilding them) gives Age of Mythology a more dramatic and fast-paced game play. Buildings aren't all powerful fortified obstacles that can only be breached by siege weapons (they do help, but are not essential) but they can form a fortified position when mutually supported by troops. The human soldiers fight in rock-paper-scissors counters: infantry with lances beat cavalry, who beats archers, that in turn beat infantry; plus specialized troops augmenting or changing such roles (archers beat infantry, but the fast running Huskarl will close-in fast and kill them). The mythological units are powerful but there are heroes in the game that will counter them. The same principle applies to naval warfare.

On the economic field, you have food, wood, gold and favor. While the first three are self-explanatory, favor is specific to this game and plays a great role: it is the protection your civilization receive from the gods. Each faction has a different way of gaining favor: the Greeks pray at the temple while the Egyptians build monuments. Each civilization has three major gods that will affect it in a particular way. At each Age you have to choose a minor god to advance, granting you a special power and a different myth unit. Gods also provide different research improvements and almost all of them cost favor. The game revolves around building and mantaining city centers, that not only provide the training of villagers, but also increase your population count and need to be built in specific and limited places; making it an strategic objective in-game.

The game has five campaigns but only the original one is good. The community does not allow discussions and is very weak in guides. Strategies, build orders... all of this must be researched outside Steam. Another problem is the lack of balance. The first expansion added the Atlanteans, that are awfully overpowered. They do not need to build resource depots (the mark of lazy design), they do not need to build any specific building for gaining favor (their city centers automatically generate favor), their buildings are stronger than everybody's and their villagers are small tanks with far more hit points - any of their units can become heroes... The Norse are the only ones to build heroes in unlimited numbers already on the Archaic Age and this leads to very cheap early rushes. The major god Loki summons myth units for Norse heroes fighting, so it is no surprise so many players pick this god. The Chinese, while not a bad faction, had such a lazy campaign, with boring missions and awfully crude cinematic (worse than the ones on the AOM original release)! Worse, the Chinese expansion changes the menu presentation and the theme music - which I hated - and does not provide an option for the traditional menu.

With those problems aside (like few people still playing the game), AOM is a great experience and I still to this day get a smile when I listen to the songs and sounds of this game (Prostagma?). The original campaign is a Tour de Force following the hero Arkantos and his friends through the myths of the ancient Greeks, Egyptians and Norse; with you fighting the Trojan War with Ajax and the like under the guidance of Athena. The visuals are great, with the gods of AOM being among the best portrayals of those mythical figures that I have ever seen. Playing this game with friends, even against the AI, is always guaranteed fun. Highly recommended.

It hurts so much to not be able to recommend this game.

Let me put this into context. When I first played Age of Mythology, I was still an Age of Empires 2 junkie, more so than I am today. I used to play all the time. Then I saw this.

Age of Mythology, for its time, featured stunning performance for wonderful 3D models and world, beautiful visual effects, more intuitive controls than ever, wildly diverse gameplay and all kinds of amazing ideas. Instant favorite among RTS games. The campaigns are wonderfully crafted, far superior to the very loosely designed AoE2 campaigns. Multiplayer was smoother than ever, custom scenarios were better and more complex, thanks to the extremely powerful editor that exists. Balance was pretty good too: although Isis had a serious upper hand. And the sountrack is still one of my favorite for the Age of Empires series, possibly one of my favorite soundtracks ever: I have it on my phone and listen to it in transport.

Yes, Age of Mythology is a spectacular game and a worthy spin-off to the Age of Empires series.

So when I saw that it was coming to Steam, tidied up and ready for new and improved multiplayer through the more stable Steam servers, I was psyched. I forked over the cash for it and the expansion and booted it up.

Or, I would have, if it had worked. On my old PC, there were a myriad of problems that made it impossible to play, while the original worked just fine. "Fair enough," I said, "the graphical improvements probably make it impossible for my old PC to keep up." I got a new PC later and tried again. And lo and behold it booted up. It didn't take long for me to find problems.

Firstly: the launcher. Like Age of Empires 2 HD, there is a useless and arbitrary launcher that you need to go through. This is a minor fault, but it comes up every single time you want to play the game. I've already clicked to launch the game via Steam, what good can this launcher possibly do?

But let's continue. I got the main menu and found another problem. The main menu, by default, was actually bugged for me and the map would display incorrectly, which had a very unpolished look. Still, a minor detail, I'm sure the rest of the game is just fine.

I went to multiplayer to get started playing games. And that's when I noticed the next problem. The main menu theme never stops playing, even as you're waiting hours in lobbies for people to join your game so you can play. And considering it's a loud minute long loop, this is not a welcome addition.

Then another problem, which I've hinted at above becomes obvious. Nobody is playing this game. I wondered why, as I eventually got a game together.

That's when I realized that lobby chat was bugged, which prevented proper scrolling. (this was later fixed) But I thought, "Ah well, at least the game will play properly."

Then the game started. Or well, I say started, but really, I got an instant desync problem and had to relaunch my game because connecting to another player is foreign technology to the AoM engine. So I launched up again, went through the last problems one more time and tried again. This time I got a game going.

The first thing that struck me was "Gee, this looks a lot like the original game." Which is nice, but then I thought about the title: "Extended Edition". About the only visual differences I could find were lighting that often bugs and glitches and looks terrible (particularly during Eclipse godpower) and very shimmery looking water. And for these two small and bordering insignificant changes, the game chugged and grinded along at a snail's pace, making the original feel like a blazing racecar of optimization and careful coding. This was just insulting. I paid full-price for a game that is practically identical to the old game except that it runs slower and desyncs more often.

During the course of the game, I also noticed that the game has a lot more glitches and bugs, with units almost regularly pathing into trees or cliffs for no discernable reason, something that never happened in the original game to my knowledge and very long playtime. Not to mention, pathing seemed quantifiably worse in general which is a shame, because the original AoM has some of the best pathing for units in any RTS game. 

So, I decided "Alright, well maybe the campaigns are different or there's a new one. And what about this Chinese expansion?"

Well, let's start with the campaigns. The original campaign is essentially unchanged, which is just as well, because it was quite good. The additional campaigns, like The Golden Gift, are present, again with no changes. And they all work as they should, so there's no issue there. But there's no visual improvements to speak of, even in grossly underdeveloped parts of the original, like the lack of facial movements in characters, which surely an Extended Edition, as the game so boldly proclaims itself to be, could fix? And then there's the Chinese campaign, which is a shoddy excuse of a campaign that feels less like an official campaign, crafted with excellence and care and more like a weekend project for a couple of die-hard fans. Check out AoM Heaven and go to campaigns. I can almost guarantee that anything there will be superior to the absolutely feeble attempt that the Chinese campaign makes at being fun or pretty or even interesting.

Then there are the Chinese civilizations. Ignoring the controversy of the minor God portraits, the Chinese civilizations are interesting in a lot of respects and would fill a very interesting role in the game. If they worked and were balanced. As an example of how ineptly programmed this expansion seems to be, the first God power for one of the Chinese Gods, which does nothing more complicated than summon a band of goats, crashes the game. Let me re-iterate this. The simple act of spawning goats. With the very first God power for a civilization. Crashes the game. This is not an obscure or far-out scenario that would never be tested, this is probably one of the first items to be checked. And yet, it was broken for months before finally being patched. And that's only one example. There are countless other Chinese-based bugs that had to be patched out. And the game STILL has pathing issues. The Chinese were extremely powerful during the initial release (and some would argue still are too strong after the fix). And considering that their main point of interest is their gardens, which are a resource generating building, they lack the interesting diversity of the other three civilizations: their villagers may as well be Greeks. If gardens had more emphasis as the main method of Chinese gathering, rather than an awkward supplement and the way to gain favor, this could have been interesting (if also difficult to balance and play). But naturally, there is a great fear in creating something different.

Now, I could forgive all of this is the dev team would respond to some of these issues with even a semblence of activity. But I have seen nothing from them. Instead, all I find are more and more expansions to AoE2. Nothing but ways to rake in more cash. And it is saddening, because I want to play AoM on Steam and I will gladly pay for the experience, but this is not AoM and it is certainly not an Extended Edition. If anything, this is a downgrade from the original, which was extremely robust.

So, let's list the problems: the game is visually difficult to distinguish from its original, the game is less solidly programmed than the original, the game has an unbalanced and buggy expansion, the dev response is pathetically slow and the game costs more than the original does most of the time. Why would you buy this game?

[h1]Short version: 75%[/h1]
Age of Mythology offers one of the best strategy game campaigns of its time; a rich, lengthy, and exciting epic using many mythological elements from various cultures. It is a spectacular single-player experience, but not really an RTS to play for too long beyond that.

[h1]Long version:[/h1]
Age of Mythology was a bold undertaking, since it stepped quite far away from the previous Age of Empires games. Not just in tone, basing itself on mythology and adding gods and monsters to its roster of units, but by also mixing up its time-tested real-time strategy formula as well.

Unlike in previous games, we can only choose from three factions (plus a fourth in the included Titans expansion). They all rely on fundamentally different mechanics in every aspect, be it the way they gather resources, their building and unit composition, or their fighting style. This kind of setup always carries several potential balance issues, and AoM has plenty of those—this is maybe why it is still less popular for multiplayer games than its older sibling, Age of Empires II.

However, it boosts the best single-player campaign in the entire franchise; a 32-stage cinematic masterpiece about an Atlantean general chasing a power-mad Cyclops through ancient Greece, Egypt, and the Norselands, before he upsets the natural order of things and dooms Atlantis. The follow-up 12-level expansion about a group of Atlantean refugees feels more haphazard in writing, although its plot manages to raise the stakes much higher, creating an intense atmosphere during the stages.
(As a bonus, we also get a 4-level Norse mini-campaign, which is okay, but not much more.)

My personal pick for greatest RTS of all time, although i know that's a highly contested category with games like AoE, C&C and Starcraft all being masterpieces in their own right. My love for Age of Mythology is partly because it's a game i played non stop as a kid being one of my first PC games, but also because it's a legendary RTS that still holds up by today's standards.

AoM is packed to the brim with unique units, gods to play, maps, a lengthy campaign and great mod support, not to mention a banger soundtrack. You have your basic RTS elements - gathering resources, building your towns, training units, expanding your territory, making war and trading with allies. Where AoM's strength lies is each time you advance through an age, say Classical to Heroic age you get to pick a new god or deity to swear allegiance to. Each of these gods gives you access to unique units, buildings, powers and more making each game feel varied depending on what you pick. 

The gods you can pick are decided by which faction you play, these factions are the Greeks, Egyptians, Norse, Atlanteans and Chinese(DLC needed). Every one of them playing completely different and require different economic, military and strategic approaches to gameplay. The Greek faction for example will require you to send your villagers to pray at temples to gain favour with the gods, the Egyptians instead build Statues and monuments to appease theirs. This small example is what you can expect on a larger scale with the different factions and even different god choices within the respective factions resulting in a really varied RTS that can always offer something different no matter the hours you have in the game.

The units are fantastic with every sort of mythical creature you can imagine making battles a spectacle of Frost Giants fighting Minotaurs and Scarabs, mixed in with your basic units such as Hoplites and Pharaohs. 
In closing AoM is a hard game to get bored of if this is your sort of thing, no bs just pure gameplay and content. A timeless classic from a time in video games which we probably will never see again.

If you are looking for a multiplayer RTS, and your internet speed isn't incredible, move along. That said, if you are interested in single player or have amazing internet connection, go right ahead. 

In Short - There is a compounded latency issue. Animation quality is directly proportional to connection quality. One player with a bad connection (Or a large number of players) will slow your game. And when it slows down your game, it slows down everything causing animations to lag and glitch. They’ve updated the server client code in the Extended Edition, where they didn't need to (causing terrible bugs).

In Long: Instead of a dedicated server setup. AOM now uses a peer to peer connection. The Pros are that you don't need to create servers, or port forward. But the downside is that the next iteration of the game cannot continue until every player has received information from every other player. 
This means that with more players, more information is required to be sent before a game iteration occurs. Additionally, with one player with a high latency, that latency affects every single player within the game. Currently with this problem, AOM game speed slows down, affecting EVERY SINGLE ELEMENT OF GAMEPLAY. This includes MODEL ANIMATION (Imagine bad connection = laggy and glitchy character models). 

However, this game would have been fine it they either: 
When the game speed is slowed down, change the timings of the model animations to match the new game speed (Just play on lightning speed to compensate).
…Or just kept the old dedicated server engine for AOM.

Age of Mythology is a spin-off of the Age of Empires franchise, focusing on mythological creatures and deities, in contrast to the more realistic approach of the main games. In this game, you can control one of four different civilizations, five if you have the DLC, and each civilization has its own major and minor gods to further diversify gameplay.

The four base civilizations are the Greek, Norse, Egyptian and Atlantean civilizations. The last one was added to the original game with the Titans expansion, though only with this Extended Edition was I able to try them out, as I never got the expansion for the original game. As I said above, beyond picking a civilization, you also get to pick a major god; think of this as a sub-civilization with its own bonuses and such. Besides that, gameplay remains mostly similar to what you'd expect from an Age of Empires game: you need to build your economy, train troops, advance ages and such. However, one of the key differences is that when advancing ages, you get to pick one of two minor deities; this feels like a precursor to Age of Empires III age-up mechanic, as each minor god offers specific bonuses. There's also god powers, one for each age, that can aid you in battle or in regards to your economy.

The game has several singleplayer campaigns; while it originally launched with a single one, the Fall of the Trident campaign, this Extended Edition includes the ones that were added later on through expansions, which are the Golden Gift campaign, and New Atlantis. The first campaign is rather extensive, featuring over 30 scenarios, and taking you through all major civs. It also makes use of cutscenes (rendered in-engine), which add a more cinematic feel compared to earlier games in the franchise. Personally, I enjoyed them all, though there's a few minor bugs here and there.

Beyond the campaign, you can play skirmish against the AI or online with other players. There's a couple of different game modes, from Supremacy, which is basically a traditional skirmish, to Deathmatch (starts with high resources and the map revealed), and even Treaty mode, which adds a timer where you can't attack, so you can build up your economy first. There's also a scenario editor so you can make up your own maps either for skirmish, or for a custom campaign.

Now, talking about the graphics, well, it has some enhancements as an "Extended Edition" compared to the original game, but it's still an early 2000s game at its core; don't expect anything ultra realistic, but at least compared to Age of Empires II, units and buildings are no longer simple sprites, but actual 3D models. The soundtrack is very nice, and each civilization gets its own theme that plays at the start of a match.

All in all, it was nice revisiting this classic from my childhood/teenage years after so long. I can recommend it, although with Retold in the horizon, you might want to wait for that one.
